label: EmArcy
rationale: The definitive jazz-vocal record and the only collaboration between Sarah Vaughan and Clifford Brown. Penguin Guide core collection with crown status ("one of the great jazz vocal records"), AllMusic 5 stars ("one of the most important jazz-meets-vocal sessions ever recorded"), Grammy Hall of Fame (1999), and Ben Ratliff's 'Jazz: A Critic's Guide to the 100 Most Important Recordings' — all documented in the Wikipedia reception section (S1). Session gravity is exceptional: Clifford Brown (trumpet), Roy Haynes (drums), Paul Quinichette (tenor), Herbie Mann (flute), Jimmy Jones (piano), Joe Benjamin (bass), with Ernie Wilkins arranging. Sarah Vaughan has no representation in the canon; this is the record a vocal-jazz gap should be closed with.

personnel_record.notes: Recorded at Fine Sound Studios, 711 Fifth Avenue, New York City, across two sessions, December 16 and 18, 1954; released 1955 (EmArcy MG-36004), reissued 1991 as 'Sarah Vaughan with Clifford Brown'. Wikipedia's infobox gives a single recording date (December 18) while Discogs gives December 16 and 18; per-track session assignment is not documented, so track-level session dates are left null. Track 10 ('Lullaby of Birdland, alternate take') is a CD-reissue bonus. Composer conflict on 'It's Crazy': Wikipedia credits Al Fields and Timmie Rogers; Discogs credits Dorothy Fields and Richard Rodgers — the Wikipedia attribution is retained (Al Fields/Timmie Rogers are the known writers of the standard) and the Discogs variant flagged here. No recording engineer is credited by either Wikipedia or Discogs; producer Bob Shad is the only original production credit, so engineer is null.

ballot.album: Sarah Vaughan — Sarah Vaughan with Clifford Brown (1954)
ballot.case_for: Four independent critical traditions converge on this record: Penguin Guide core collection with crown designation, AllMusic 5 stars, Grammy Hall of Fame (1999), and Ben Ratliff's Critic's Guide to the 100 Most Important Recordings — a consensus density matched by very few albums in the canon. It is simultaneously Vaughan's definitive small-group studio session and one of the last great documents of Clifford Brown's trumpet playing, recorded eighteen months before his death at 25. The session gravity is extraordinary: Brown, Roy Haynes, Paul Quinichette, Herbie Mann, Jimmy Jones, Joe Benjamin, and arranger Ernie Wilkins constitute a complete elite hard-bop ensemble, anchoring a vocal date deep in the instrumental tradition the canon is built on. Vaughan currently has zero representation; this is the record that closes that gap.
ballot.case_against: The substantive critique is sourcing depth: every reception claim — Penguin crown, Grammy HoF, Ratliff, AllMusic — routes through a single Wikipedia reception section (S1), with the remaining sources (Discogs, iTunes, MusicBrainz) confirming only credits and catalog data. A dossier this strong should ideally cite the Penguin Guide entry, the Grammy listing, and Ratliff's book directly rather than aggregating them through one secondary source. The secondary tension is center-of-gravity: the canon's spine is instrumental post-bop, and admitting a vocal-led date sets a precedent for how much vocal jazz the collection should carry — not a case against this album, but a horizon question John should weigh.
ballot.recommendation: Admit at consensus_core / must_have, but upgrade the dossier's reception sourcing from a single Wikipedia section to direct citations before final inclusion.
